title: The Professional Passive Reconnaissance Framework
introduction: A framework is not a checklist you follow mechanically. It is a mental model for how information flows — from 'I know nothing about this target' to 'I know exactly where to focus my testing.' The five-phase framework below is what professional penetration testers, red teamers, and bug bounty hunters use, in slightly different forms, across every engagement. Understanding the phases and why they exist in this order is more valuable than memorising the tools in each.

sections.heading: Phase 1: Scope and Planning — before touching any tool
sections.content:
The scope document is the most important document in a penetration test. It defines what you are authorised to do, against which assets, and under what conditions. Reading it thoroughly before any information gathering is not optional — it is the professional baseline.

What to extract from the scope document:

**In-scope assets**: domains, IP ranges, web applications, cloud accounts. Build a complete list. These are the only systems you have authorisation to test.

**Out-of-scope assets**: systems explicitly excluded. Common exclusions: third-party hosted services, CDN infrastructure (Cloudflare, Akamai), payment processors, specific production databases. Knowing what is excluded is as important as knowing what is included.

**Rules of Engagement (RoE)**: when testing is authorised (business hours only? 24/7?), what notification is required before certain test types, who to contact if a critical finding is discovered, emergency stop conditions.

**Timeline**: how many days for passive recon? When does active testing begin? When is the report due? This determines the depth of passive reconnaissance that is feasible.

**Planning output**: before any tool is opened, write a reconnaissance plan. One page is enough:
— List of all in-scope domains
— List of all in-scope IP ranges
— Priority order (which assets to investigate first and why — usually the primary business domain, then any subdomains, then IP ranges)
— Reconnaissance techniques authorised (always passive OSINT; sometimes active — confirm in RoE)
— Documentation standards (how findings will be recorded)

callout.title: Never start without reading the scope document
callout.content: This sounds obvious. It is violated constantly. Testers who are excited to begin open their tools before finishing the scope document. The result: they investigate assets that are out of scope, miss assets that are in scope, and sometimes perform actions that violate the Rules of Engagement. The scope document is read completely, before any information gathering begins, on every professional engagement. No exceptions.

sections.heading: Phase 2: Passive Information Gathering — in sequence
sections.content:
Passive information gathering is performed in a specific sequence. The sequence matters because each phase builds on the last — later phases use information discovered in earlier ones.

**Step 1: Registration intelligence (WHOIS).**
For each in-scope domain: who registered it, when, which registrar, which nameservers, whether WHOIS privacy is active. The registration date tells you how old the infrastructure is. The nameserver identifies the DNS hosting provider. WHOIS privacy tells you whether the organisation actively manages its public exposure.

**Step 2: DNS enumeration.**
For each in-scope domain and each subdomain found: query all eight record types (A, AAAA, MX, NS, TXT, CNAME, PTR, SRV). Identify email provider (MX), CDN relationships (NS, CNAME), email security posture (DMARC p= value from TXT), cloud vendor disclosures (TXT verification tokens), and direct IP addresses (A records on subdomains not behind CDN). Attempt zone transfer on self-managed nameservers (active — confirm authorisation). Enumerate subdomains via Certificate Transparency (crt.sh) and wordlist brute force.

**Step 3: Search engine reconnaissance.**
For each in-scope domain: site: overview, filetype: document search (pdf, xlsx, docx, env), intitle:"index of" directory listings, inurl: portal discovery, robots.txt review, sitemap.xml review, Wayback Machine historical snapshots, GitHub and Pastebin credential searches, Shodan infrastructure intelligence (if organisational IP ranges are in scope).

**Step 4: Supplementary OSINT (where applicable).**
LinkedIn and social media: employee names, job roles, technology mentioned in job postings. Job advertisements: technology stack disclosure ('experience with AWS Lambda, PostgreSQL, and React required'). Company news: recent acquisitions (new infrastructure), breaches (pre-existing vulnerabilities to check), system migrations (legacy infrastructure still live). Regulatory filings: publicly filed documents sometimes contain network or infrastructure detail.

callout.title: Why the sequence matters
callout.content: WHOIS first because it establishes scope validation — confirming the domain is actually owned by the target organisation. DNS enumeration second because it expands the scope (revealing subdomains to add to the investigation list) before search engine recon is performed on domains that may not yet be known. Search engine recon last because it references specific subdomains and IP addresses found in the DNS phase. Running them out of order means search engine queries reference an incomplete subdomain list.

sections.heading: Phase 3: Intelligence Analysis — connecting the dots
sections.content:
Raw findings are not intelligence. A list of DNS records, a list of Google results, and a list of WHOIS data is not an intelligence picture — it is a collection of notes. Intelligence analysis is the work of understanding what the findings mean together.

The intelligence analysis questions to answer:

**What is the full asset inventory?** List every domain, subdomain, and IP address that belongs to the target and was discovered during passive recon — including those not in the original scope document (flag these separately).

**What does the infrastructure architecture look like?** Is the main website behind a CDN? Which subdomains are directly reachable? Are there multiple hosting providers (suggesting infrastructure evolution rather than deliberate design)? Is there a clear DMZ/separation between public and internal-facing systems?

**What technology stack is running?** Email platform (Google/Microsoft/self-hosted). CRM (Salesforce tokens in TXT). CDN provider (NS records). Cloud platform (ASN analysis, Shodan). Application server (page headers, error messages, cached pages). Version information (metadata, Shodan banners, cached page footers).

**What is the email security posture?** SPF record: which vendors are authorised to send email? DMARC p= value: can the domain be spoofed? DKIM: is per-message signing in place?

**What findings have multiple confirming sources?** A finding confirmed by three independent passive sources (e.g., Salesforce confirmed by TXT record + portal CNAME + SPF include) is established fact. A single-source finding is a hypothesis to verify during active testing.

callout.title: The correlation principle
callout.content: In intelligence analysis, corroboration is confidence. If WHOIS says the organisation uses GoDaddy, the NS records say the DNS is on Cloudflare, and a job posting says they are hiring a 'Cloudflare specialist,' three independent passive sources agree on the same infrastructure detail. That finding is solid. A finding supported by a single source — a single DNS record, a single Google result — is plausible but needs corroboration before it drives major decisions.

sections.heading: Phase 4: Attack Surface Mapping — organising what you found
sections.content:
The attack surface is the complete set of entry points an attacker could use to attempt access to the target. The intelligence analysis phase identified everything; the attack surface mapping phase organises it by relevance to active testing.

A professional attack surface map categorises every finding into four tiers:

**Critical (immediate escalation or highest-priority active testing):**
— Unauthenticated endpoints returning live data
— Credentials discovered in passive sources (GitHub, Pastebin)
— Open directories containing database backups or configuration files
— Active phishing domains or impersonation infrastructure targeting the organisation

**High (prioritised active testing):**
— Development or staging servers with direct IPs (no CDN protection)
— Admin portals publicly accessible via internet
— DMARC p=none (domain spoofable in phishing)
— Legacy subdomains with direct IPs running older software

**Medium (active testing, normal priority):**
— CDN-protected IP addresses (harder to reach but still in-scope)
— Cloud vendor disclosures (useful for attack path planning in active phase)
— Document metadata findings (employee names, directory structures)
— Exposed login portals with unknown software versions

**Low (documented, lower testing priority):**
— Standard WHOIS and DNS registration data
— Email provider identification
— Technology stack inference from job postings
— Historical Wayback Machine data

callout.title: The attack surface map guides active testing
callout.content: When active testing begins on Monday, Maya does not start with the main Cloudflare-protected website. She starts with the dev.meridian-financial.com Vultr VPS — a direct IP, potentially running older software, likely less monitored, almost certainly sharing the same application codebase as production. The attack surface map told her that is the highest-priority target. Without the map, that decision requires guess work. With it, it is the obvious starting point.

sections.heading: Phase 5: Documentation and Reporting — making the work professional
sections.content:
A reconnaissance finding without documentation is not a professional finding. It is a memory — which fades, which cannot be shared with a client, which cannot be referred to in a court proceeding if the engagement produces legal questions.

Every passive reconnaissance finding must be documented at the time of discovery with:

**Source**: exactly which tool, query, or URL produced the finding. Example: 'Google Dork query: site:meridian-financial.com intitle:"index of" — performed 2026-08-04 14:32 UTC — returned directory at meridian-financial.com/backup/'

**Evidence**: the raw result. A screenshot for visual findings (Google results, directory listings). A text copy of DNS query output. The URL and HTTP response code for accessible pages. The metadata output from ExifTool.

**Severity**: Critical, High, Medium, or Low — based on the attack surface mapping criteria.

**Recommended Action**: what the client should do to remediate. For p=none DMARC: 'Implement DMARC policy of p=quarantine or p=reject to prevent domain spoofing in phishing campaigns.' For an open directory: 'Disable directory listing on web server and remove the /backup/ directory from the document root or apply access controls.'

The reconnaissance section of a professional penetration test report is written before active testing begins. It is a standalone deliverable that the client can act on — and often should act on, when critical findings are present — before the active phase is complete.

keyTerms.definition: The contractual document defining which assets are authorised for testing, what actions are permitted, the timeline, and the Rules of Engagement. Read completely before any information gathering begins.
The specific conditions governing a penetration test engagement: authorised hours, notification requirements, emergency contacts, and conditions requiring the test to stop.
The phase of reconnaissance where raw findings are correlated to produce a coherent picture of the target's infrastructure, technology stack, and security posture.
The complete set of entry points through which an attacker could attempt to access a target system. The attack surface map prioritises these entry points for active testing.

The principle that findings supported by multiple independent passive sources are more reliable than single-source findings. A three-source corroborated finding is established fact; a single-source finding is a hypothesis.
